section_summary: This section covers U.S. State Department despatches, memoranda, and background reports from late 1934 to early 1935 concerning political, military, and economic developments in Japan under the Okada Cabinet. The documents examine internal factional divisions within the major political parties (Seiyukai and Minseito), the growing political ascendancy and regimentation campaigns of the military under War Minister Senjuro Hayashi, and international economic frictions. Extensive analyses by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew explore the demographic, agrarian, and industrial pressures fueling Japan's urge toward expansion in East Asia, proposing a dual American strategy of military preparedness combined with sympathetic economic accommodation.

subfiles.about: Concluding pages of Despatch No. 908 examining factional conflict in the Seiyukai, parliamentary relations with the Minseito and House of Peers, and political prospects for the Okada Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This concluding portion of Despatch No. 908 analyzes internal factional strife within the majority Seiyukai party, notably the Tokonami and Kuhara factions' tensions with party president Dr. Suzuki following Tokonami's entry into the Okada Cabinet. It reviews the minority Minseito's cooperation with the administration and the cool reception accorded Admiral Okada by dominant groups in the House of Peers. Ambassador Grew examines the likelihood of a special Diet session and possible dissolution over agrarian relief and defense budgets, concluding that Japanese politics remains in flux between bureaucratic-authoritarian tendencies and parliamentary constitutionalism.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 908: Internal Political Situation in Japan and the Position of the Okada Cabinet

subfiles.about: A confidential State Department background report analyzing Japan's constitutional structure, domestic economic depression, export trade expansion, and foreign relations with major powers.
subfiles.from: Division of Current Information, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Information Series No. 28 provides an overview of Japan's constitutional governance, underscoring the military's constitutional independence from Cabinet control. The report reviews prolonged agrarian distress and financial crises that discredited party politicians and paved the way for military dominance following the 1931 Manchurian incident. It further details Japan's state-coordinated industrial efficiency and export boom, commercial disputes and agreements with India and the Netherlands East Indies, border and fishery tensions with the Soviet Union, and key bilateral issues with the United States regarding naval parity and immigration laws.
subfiles.title: Information Series No. 28: Japan

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 1068 regarding the announced coalition between the Seiyukai and Minseito parties.
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Turner summarizes Despatch 1068 on a Seiyukai-Minseito coalition statement, judging it a temporary truce for public favor rather than policy agreement, since the Seiyukai opposes Okada's government while Minseito supports it.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1068 Regarding Position of Political Parties in Japan
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on the joint coalition announcement by the Seiyukai and Minseito ahead of the special Diet session and the internal party split over Korekiyo Takahashi joining the Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1068 assesses the public resurgence of Japanese political parties and examines the joint coalition manifesto published by the Seiyukai and Minseito prior to the extraordinary session of the Diet on November 28, 1934. Ambassador Grew highlights the divergent stances of Seiyukai leader Dr. Suzuki, who fiercely attacked the government, and Minseito manager Chuji Machida, who pledged continued cooperation with Okada. The dispatch also details the Seiyukai's decision to force former party president Korekiyo Takahashi to sever his party ties after accepting the post of Finance Minister.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1068: Position of the Political Parties in Japan

subfiles.about: Memorandum submitting and commenting on Tokyo Despatch No. 1079 regarding surging nationalism and the risks of war in Japan.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck sends Hull Despatch 1079, highlighting Neville's analysis that Japan's intensifying superpatriotism could suddenly break restraints and spark conflict, though war seems improbable for now.
subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Secretary of State on Tokyo Despatch No. 1079: Recent Political Tendencies in Japan

subfiles.about: Despatch analyzing the historical roots of Japanese nationalism, current movements for economic self-sufficiency, and military opposition to foreign enterprise.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew (drafted by Edwin L. Neville), U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1079, drafted by Counselor Edwin L. Neville, examines Japan's wave of nationalism through the lens of historical cycles alternating between foreign borrowing and national seclusion. Neville reports that military and ultranationalist circles, convinced that Western civilization has little left to teach Japan, are pushing aggressively for national self-sufficiency in key industries. The dispatch documents how military pressure obstructed General Motors' expansion in Osaka and fueled petroleum market restrictions, leaving moderate business leaders helpless in the face of national hysteria.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1079: Recent Political Tendencies in Japan

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Berlin Despatch No. 1611 regarding an interview with the Japanese War Minister in the Nazi press.
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Turner summarizes a Berlin-relayed interview with War Minister Hayashi explaining his controversial memorandum aimed at educating the public on Japan's world-power duties and wartime preparation without abruptly upending the social order.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Berlin Despatch No. 1611: Interview with Japanese War Minister
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting translated excerpts of an interview with Japanese War Minister General Senjuro Hayashi published in the Nazi organ Völkischer Beobachter.
subfiles.from: John Campbell White, Chargé d'Affaires a.i., U.S. Embassy, Berlin
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1611 encloses translated excerpts from an interview granted by War Minister Senjuro Hayashi to the Völkischer Beobachter regarding the Japanese War Ministry's memorandum on national defense. Hayashi insists the program does not contemplate sudden domestic or foreign radicalism, but rather aims to unite the ethical and material forces of the state for modern technical warfare. He discusses Japan's tenfold increase in continental defense responsibilities after establishing Manchukuo, advocates expanding air defense, endorses a 17-year military service term, and praises the unified national spirit of Nazi Germany.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1611: Interview of Voelkischer Beobachter with Japanese War Minister

subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Tokyo Despatch 1102 notes numerous dictatorship plots symptomatic of acute political turmoil in Japan.
subfiles.title: Document File Note for Tokyo Despatch No. 1102: Plots to Set Up Dictatorships

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing and analyzing Ambassador Grew's Despatch No. 1156 on the socioeconomic causes of Japanese expansionism.
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman and Stanley K. Hornbeck, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Memo reviews Grew's Despatch 1156 on Japan's expansionist social/economic drivers, recommending U.S. policy combine Far East defense readiness with sympathetic cooperation, since trade restrictions heighten aggression risk; recommends sending it to Roosevelt.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1156: Urge toward Expansion in Japan
subfiles.to: Under Secretary William Phillips and Secretary of State Cordell Hull

subfiles.about: Comprehensive diplomatic despatch analyzing the demographic, economic, and psychological forces behind Japanese expansionism and proposing a dual U.S. strategic policy.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: In Despatch No. 1156, Ambassador Grew presents an extensive examination of Japanese expansionism from the Japanese internal perspective, identifying four key driving factors: rapid population growth, scarce natural resources, industrialization, and rising living standards. He demonstrates that emigration and agricultural expansion cannot absorb the annual million-person increase, forcing Japan into mass-production export industries that are now encountering Western trade barriers and imperial blocs. Arguing that these pressures create an explosive dynamic, Grew invokes Secretary Hull's vision of economic contentment as essential to peace and recommends a two-pronged American policy: robust military preparedness to defend U.S. interests combined with international economic accommodation to provide Japan peaceful elbow-room.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1156: Urge toward Expansion in Japan

subfiles.about: A five-page digest summarizing Ambassador Grew's Despatch No. 1156 on the root causes of Japan's expansionist urge and alternative Western policies.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: This five-page digest condenses Ambassador Grew's Despatch No. 1156, systematically reviewing the four driving factors of overpopulation, lack of natural resources, industrialization, and rising living standards. It emphasizes that Japanese industrial inroads stem from discipline, technical efficiency, and national zeal, and that blocking Japanese commerce risks catastrophic conflict. The digest frames the dilemma facing Western powers as either preparing to crush Japan militarily every few generations or accommodating Japanese economic expansion while maintaining steady diplomatic pressure for demilitarization and Far Eastern stability.
subfiles.title: Digest of Tokyo Despatch No. 1156: Urge toward Expansion in Japan
subfiles.to: Secretary of State Cordell Hull and President Franklin D. Roosevelt

subfiles.about: Letter from Secretary of State Cordell Hull transmitting Ambassador Grew's despatch and digest on Japanese expansionism to President Roosevelt.
subfiles.summary: Hull sends Roosevelt Grew's Despatch 1156 and digest on Japan's expansion pressures, endorsing combining defense readiness with sympathetic cooperation, noting the administration already sought such cooperation where practicable.
subfiles.title: Letter from Secretary of State Cordell Hull to President Franklin D. Roosevelt Transmitting Tokyo Despatch No. 1156 and Digest
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States
